stem:
Table 1 shows the percentage of the population living in urban areas in three fictional countries (fictional data).

| Country | 1980 | 2020 |
|---|---|---|
| A (HIC) | 74 | 82 |
| B (MIC) | 35 | 61 |
| C (LIC) | 12 | 30 |

Resource: on the edge of the largest city of Country C, an unplanned settlement has grown on steep land beside a river. Homes are built of scrap metal and plastic sheeting, there are few toilets, and water is bought from vendors.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the change in the percentage urban in Country B between 1980 and 2020 (in percentage points).

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Which country had the smallest increase in its percentage urban?

options.content: All rose by the same amount

options.rationale: Correct: it rose by only 8 points (74 to 82).

parts.explanation: HICs are already highly urbanised, so growth is slow.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why the rate of urban growth is slow in HICs such as Country A.

points.description: Most people already live in towns, so few rural people are left to migrate.
Low birth rates mean little natural increase in cities.
Counter-urbanisation: some people move from cities to rural areas or small towns.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Most people in A already live in towns, so few remain in rural areas to migrate; birth rates are low; and some city dwellers move out to the countryside.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain the causes of rapid urban growth in LICs such as Country C.

points.description: Rural-urban migration due to push factors (poverty, drought, lack of land, few services).
Pull factors: jobs (including informal), higher wages, schools, hospitals in cities.
High natural increase in cities: many young migrants of child-bearing age; high birth rates.
Falling death rates in cities due to better health care, adding to growth.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Rural people are pushed out by poverty, drought and land shortage and pulled to cities by jobs, higher wages and better schools and hospitals. Because most migrants are young adults, they have children in the city, and with better health care death rates are low, so natural increase adds greatly to growth.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Using the resource, describe **three** characteristics of the unplanned settlement.

points.description: Built on unsafe land (steep slopes, beside a river - risk of landslides or floods).
Homes of scrap or temporary materials (metal, plastic sheeting).
Poor services: few toilets, no piped water (water bought from vendors).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: It is on steep land by a river, homes are made of scrap metal and plastic, and there are few toilets and no piped water.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Describe **three** opportunities of urban living for migrants arriving in the city.

points.description: More jobs, in both formal and informal sectors, and higher incomes.
Better access to schools, hospitals and clinics.
Electricity, water, entertainment, transport / chance to send remittances home.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Migrants can find work, even informal jobs such as trading, and earn more than in rural areas; children can attend better schools; and health care, electricity and transport are easier to reach.

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: Describe the impacts of urban sprawl on the rural-urban fringe.

points.description: Loss of farmland and natural habitats to housing, roads and industry.
Rising land prices / farmers sell land; traffic and pollution increase.
Unplanned settlements or out-of-town developments spread; services overstretched; dumping of waste.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: As the city spreads, farmland and woodland are built over, land prices rise and traffic and pollution increase, while unplanned settlements and illegal dumping spread on the edge.

parts.label: (h)
parts.stem: For a named urban area in an LIC or MIC, describe the challenges caused by its rapid growth. You should refer to a detailed specific example.

points.description: Names the city and gives its context (e.g. Mumbai, India: one of the world's largest cities).
Causes of growth: migration from rural states / natural increase.
Housing: unplanned settlements such as Dharavi, overcrowded, on marginal land.
Water and sanitation: shortages, shared toilets, water-borne disease.
Traffic congestion and overcrowded trains; air pollution.
Waste: large dumps, uncollected refuse; flooding when drains block (e.g. 2005 floods).
Employment: many in informal work with low, insecure incomes; inequality.

levels.descriptor: Developed, accurate explanation of several relevant points, supported by a located example or the resource, with a clear judgement or conclusion where the question asks for one.
Some explanation of relevant points, partly developed; an example or resource evidence is used in general terms; any judgement is simple or one-sided.
Simple statements or a list of points with little explanation; no example or only a name.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Mumbai in India has grown rapidly because of migration from poorer rural states and high natural increase, and its urban area now holds many millions of people (approximate). A large share of people live in unplanned settlements such as Dharavi, one of Asia's largest, where houses are crowded close together, many families share toilets and water supply is limited, so water-borne diseases spread. Roads are badly congested and suburban trains are severely overcrowded, adding to air pollution. Refuse collection cannot keep up, so waste piles up at large dumps and blocks drains, which made the 2005 floods worse. Many residents work in the informal sector with low, insecure incomes, while the city also has very wealthy areas, so inequality is great. Rapid growth has therefore created challenges for housing, services, transport and the environment.

parts.explanation: A detailed specific example of the challenges of urban growth.

explanation: A Cambridge Paper 2 topic 7 question: urban growth rates, causes of growth in LICs, unplanned settlements, sprawl and a named city's challenges.
hints: Think about migration and natural increase.

stem:
Resource: a fictional city in an MIC has introduced three strategies to manage its rapid growth: (1) a bus rapid transit (BRT) system with dedicated bus lanes; (2) upgrading of an unplanned settlement by laying water pipes, building toilet blocks and giving residents legal title; (3) a green belt around the city.

Table 1 shows average morning journey times on one main route (fictional data).

| | Before BRT | After BRT |
|---|---|---|
| By bus (minutes) | 75 | 45 |
| By car (minutes) | 58 | 52 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage reduction in bus journey time after the BRT opened.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: What is the main purpose of a green belt?

options.content: To provide space for new factories
options.rationale: Industry is restricted in green belts.

options.content: To house migrants in new settlements
options.rationale: Housing is restricted in green belts.

options.content: To limit urban sprawl into the countryside
options.rationale: Correct: building is strictly controlled in the belt.

options.content: To widen roads into the city centre
options.rationale: Green belts are about land use, not roads.

parts.explanation: Green belts protect open land around a city.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Using Table 1, explain why BRT can reduce traffic congestion.

points.description: Dedicated lanes let buses avoid traffic, so bus journeys are much faster (75 to 45 minutes).
Faster buses persuade some car users to switch to public transport.
Fewer cars on the road, so car journeys also become slightly faster (58 to 52 minutes).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: With their own lanes, buses avoid jams and journey times fell from 75 to 45 minutes, so some drivers switch to the bus and fewer cars use the road; car times also fell from 58 to 52 minutes.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain why upgrading an unplanned settlement may be better than demolishing it.

points.description: Residents keep their homes, jobs and community networks close by.
Cheaper than building new housing for everyone.
Legal title gives security, so residents invest in improving their homes.
Water pipes and toilets reduce disease quickly / demolition makes people homeless and they rebuild elsewhere.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Upgrading lets people stay near their jobs and neighbours, costs far less than new housing, and legal title encourages them to improve their homes. Piped water and toilets cut disease, whereas demolition leaves people homeless and they simply build elsewhere.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Describe how a site-and-service scheme works.

points.description: The authority provides plots of land.
Plots have basic services (water, sewer connections, roads, sometimes electricity).
Residents build their own houses, often gradually, sometimes with low-cost loans or a small rent.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The city provides serviced plots with water, sewerage and access roads, and families build their own homes on them as they can afford, sometimes with small loans.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Describe **four** features of a sustainable city.

points.description: Efficient public transport, cycle lanes and walkable neighbourhoods.
Renewable energy and energy-efficient buildings.
Waste reduction, recycling and composting; water conservation and recycling.
Green spaces / affordable housing and services for all / local participation in decisions.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A sustainable city has good public transport and cycle lanes, uses solar and other renewable energy, recycles waste and water, and has green spaces and affordable housing for everyone.

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: Suggest **two** reasons why strategies like these may fail in an LIC or MIC city.

points.description: Lack of money / high cost of building and maintaining schemes.
Population grows faster than schemes can be provided / corruption / poor people cannot afford the plots or fares.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The city may lack funds to build and maintain them, and growth may outpace what is provided.

parts.label: (h)
parts.stem: For a named urban area, evaluate the strategies used to manage its growth. You should refer to a detailed specific example.

points.description: Names the urban area and the growth problems it faces (e.g. Harare: housing, water, transport, waste).
Housing strategy described (e.g. site-and-service schemes, upgrading, satellite towns such as Chitungwiza).
Evaluation of housing strategy (e.g. demand exceeds supply; unplanned settlements such as Epworth persist).
Water and sanitation strategy and its success or limits (e.g. treatment works, boreholes; shortages remain).
Transport strategy and evaluation (e.g. buses, road improvements; congestion from minibuses).
Waste management strategy and evaluation (e.g. collection, recycling; illegal dumping).
Supported overall judgement on how successful management has been.

levels.descriptor: Developed, accurate explanation of several relevant points, supported by a located example or the resource, with a clear judgement or conclusion where the question asks for one.
Some explanation of relevant points, partly developed; an example or resource evidence is used in general terms; any judgement is simple or one-sided.
Simple statements or a list of points with little explanation; no example or only a name.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Harare, Zimbabwe's capital, has grown rapidly through rural-urban migration and natural increase. To house people, the city has used site-and-service schemes, where plots with water and sewer connections are provided for families to build on, and satellite towns such as Chitungwiza, which house many workers who commute to Harare. These have provided homes for many, but demand has always exceeded supply, and unplanned or partly planned settlements such as Epworth have continued to grow on the edge of the city. Water treatment has not kept pace with the population, so many suburbs rely on boreholes and water vendors; the failure of water and sewage systems contributed to the 2008-2009 cholera outbreak. Commuter buses and minibuses carry most people, but congestion in the CBD is severe. Refuse collection is irregular, and illegal dumping is common. Overall, management has achieved some successes in housing but has not kept up with growth, mainly because of a lack of funds, so challenges remain.

parts.explanation: A detailed specific example of managing urban growth.

explanation: A Cambridge Paper 2 topic 7 question: transport, upgrading, site-and-service, green belts, sustainable cities and an evaluation of a named city's management.
hints: Upgrading improves homes where people already live.
